rationale: A wins because it stays disciplined where this update most tempts overclaiming: the unfinished clinic study. Its line, “Weak by design — the study is ongoing with nothing to report,” is exactly the grown-up answer. B is useful, but “Why athletes and biohackers are the test market for blood-oxygen sleep tracking” turns a marketing audience into a market thesis without proof. That is how founders end up pitching vibes in a blazer.
gaps_in_A: “now reacts to snoring by changing the bed's temperature” overstates the causal loop. The update says the product tracks SpO2/snoring and adjusts temperature automatically; it does not prove snoring specifically triggers the change.
“the existing owner being asked to pay again” is sharp, but it assumes an existing-owner conflict before proving whether current owners already have the sensors or whether new hardware is required.

“the same signals doctors use to screen for sleep apnea” is plausible beat context, but sleep apnea is not in the supplied update. It needs clinician/regulatory validation before becoming a factual spine.
gaps_in_B: “Why athletes and biohackers are the test market for blood-oxygen sleep tracking” is the weak slot. The facts say Eight Sleep markets to athletes and biohackers; they do not say this cohort is a test market or that users will parse SpO2 trends.
“the cohort most willing to pay premium prices and parse overnight SpO2 trends” is invented customer psychology. Marketing target is not buyer proof, and buyer proof is the whole angle.

“Right now the partnership is a logo, not a story” is too dismissive. The no-results clinic study is not a validation story, but it can be a legitimate study-design or ‘what would it take’ trade story.
“incumbent/category-power protagonist” is jargon wearing a fake mustache. The update says privately held premium product; it does not establish category power.
